script.name: Community-acquired pneumonia

epidemiology.who: Adults living in the community; risk rises with age and chronic lung disease

script.pathophysiology: Infection of the lung parenchyma, usually after aspiration of upper airway organisms. Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause; others include Haemophilus influenzae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, respiratory viruses, Staphylococcus aureus and Legionella.

timeline.course: Most patients improve within 48 to 72 hours of appropriate antibiotics

imaging: chest X-ray showing a new lobar or focal infiltrate

criteria: compatible symptoms plus a new infiltrate on chest imaging

first_line: outpatient without comorbidities: amoxicillin or doxycycline (a macrolide only where pneumococcal macrolide resistance is below 25%)
outpatient with comorbidities: amoxicillin-clavulanate or a cephalosporin plus a macrolide or doxycycline, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone alone
inpatient, not severe: ceftriaxone plus azithromycin, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone alone
next_line: add MRSA or Pseudomonas coverage only with prior isolation of those organisms or other validated risk factors

confused_with.how_to_tell_apart: Pulmonary embolism also causes pleuritic pain, dyspnea and tachycardia, but usually has clear lungs and a near-normal chest X-ray despite hypoxemia; suspect it when there are risk factors for clots.
Heart failure gives bilateral crackles, a raised JVP, leg edema and a high BNP, with bilateral interstitial edema and effusions on X-ray rather than a focal consolidation, and usually no fever.

pearls: CURB-65 (confusion, urea over 19 mg/dL, respiratory rate 30 or more, low blood pressure, age 65 or older) is a quick bedside guide to admission; the ATS/IDSA guideline prefers the Pneumonia Severity Index.

sources.title: Diagnosis and Treatment of Adults with Community-acquired Pneumonia: An Official Clinical Practice Guideline of the ATS and IDSA (2019)
